newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Jospin says not bound to EMU stability pact.
newsitem.headline: French Jospin says not bound to EMU stability pact.

text.p: French Socialist party boss Lionel Jospin said in an interview published on Tuesday there was no reason why he should feel committed to the "stability pact" on deficit control after the launch of European monetary union.

Jospin, whose party is fighting the centre-right government for power in a parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1 and has repeatedly questioned the rigour of the Maastricht treaty criteria for monetary union, said the stability pact amounted to an "absurd" concession to Germany by France's ruling coalition.

"The stability pact adds conditions which do not feature in the Maastricht treaty. The pact is a 'super-Maastricht' of sorts and a concession which the French government made absurdly to the Germans or certain German circles," Jospin told Le Monde.
"Therefore, I have no reason to feel committed to it," he told the afternoon daily.
"There are more than three million unemployed people in France and there are more than four million in Germany; no inflation in France, nor in Germany," Jospin said.
"So let's not apply economic policies which were designed for times past. The imbalance is on the demand and growth side."
"I do not see why Europe should continue, for another 10 or 15 years, to be an economic low-pressure zone compared to the other major economic regions," he said.
Jospin accused Prime Minister Alain Juppe's ruling coalition of being too timid on European affairs and said his party would seek a discussion on the way forward in the European Union.
"I want a French government which will be less timid and less passive on the European level," Jospin said.
"We've got a government which shows a lack of punch in Europe by taking a docile line on the demands of others."
The Socialists wanted a "reasonable discussion" with France's partners and no one was seeking a clash, he said.
Jospin said that the Socialists would demonstrate that they wanted a "genuine European policy" but there was no reason to believe their position would lead to crises.
"Nobody wants a crisis with France and France will not have to start one, but it will play a heftier role than it has so far," Jospin said.

Jospin's party spelled out early in the election campaign that it was against a dogmatic and arithmetical application of the deficit-curbing and other economic fitness criteria in the Maastricht Treaty and that it wanted Italy and Spain in economic and monetary union from the start.

They also argue for an "economic government" alongside the future European central bank to give a more political dimension to the monetary union project and say the euro single currency should not be overvalued against the dollar and yen.
